newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: FEATURE - Nicaragua does political u-turn, left in tatters.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Nicaragua does political u-turn, left in tatters.

text.p: Nicaragua, darling of the Latin American left in the 1980s when the Sandinista Front was in power, has taken a sharp turn to the right in the capitalist 1990s.
"The left's failure here in the 1980s was complete. There is no serious, organised leftwing force left in Nicaragua today," political analyst and former Sandinista Oscar Rene Vargas told Reuters.

Nicaragua, now in the run-up to presidential elections on Oct. 20, was home to one of Latin America's rare successful left-wing revolutions in 1979 when Sandinista guerrillas toppled the Somoza family dictatorship that had ruled with an iron fist for more than 40 years. With Soviet and Cuban backing, the Sandinistas carried out a socialist transformation of Nicaraguan society, confiscating private property and thumbing their nose at the United States.

During the heyday of the revolution, North American and European socialists, dubbed "Sandalistas" for their hippy-style footwear, flooded Nicaragua to support the revolution. But with the collapse of the Soviet Union and the Sandinista's stunning election loss to President Violeta Chamorro in 1990, Nicaragua's left has fallen on hard times.

In offices bare of amenities exept for a table and a few rickety chairs, Eli Altamirano, the Nicaraguan Communist Party's (PCN) presidential candidate, lamented the plight of the country's Marxists. "It would be a lie to say the recent changes haven't been hard on us. Nicaragua is not the same anymore," he said.

As the election approaches, rabidly anti-Sandinista rightwing candidate Arnoldo Aleman tops the polls to be Nicaragua's next president. The far-left Marxist-Leninist Party (MAP-ML) and Revolutionary Workers Party (PRT) will not even field presidential candidates, and Altamirano got only 0.1 percent of the vote in the most recent CID-Gallup poll.
But perhaps the toughest blow has been the Sandinista's apparent move to the political centre in an attempt to win the upcoming election. Polls put them in a close second to Aleman.

"The international reality has changed and the Sandinista Front has changed with it," said Daniel Ortega, the longtime Sandinista leader and the party's presidential candidate. With their recent acceptance into Socialist International, which groups the world's social democratic political parties, they are selling a new image as a democratic centre-left party willing to work with private enterprise and foreign investors.
"The Sandinistas had a leftist discourse in the 1980s but since then they have steadily shifted to the right. Their political leadership now no longer represents a left-wing option," Vargas said.

To improve their relations with the United States, the "new-look" Sandinistas have even dropped their anti-American party anthem that contained the phrase, "The Yankee is the enemy of humanity." Ardent Sandinistas now sing a Spanish-language version of Beethoven's "Ode to Joy," which talks of peace and brotherhood.

When the Sandinistas lost power in 1990, they left an economy in shambles after eight years of civil war against U.S.-backed Contra rebels and 11 years of failed economic polices. Before leaving office, party leaders transferred a still-disputed number of properties and businesses confiscated from private citizens to their own names. With these new riches, the Sandinista leadership lost much of its credibility and became part of a new dominant class, Vargas said.
"These Sandinistas became bankers, industrialists, businessmen, and owners of sugar mills and large tracts of land," he said.
This, coupled with the end of Soviet and Cuban aid, left Nicaragua's leftists on the political sidelines.

"What remains of the left can be found in sectors of the MAP-ML, the PRT and maybe among the ashes of the Sandinista Front," said Moises Hassan, former Sandinista commander and presidential candidate for the Renovating Action Movement.
